stem: Why can feature scaling materially affect k-nearest neighbors (k-NN)?

options.A: Distance calculations can be dominated by high-magnitude features, changing which points count as neighbors.
options.B: k-NN automatically rescales every feature using the target labels.
options.C: Scaling changes the number of classes.
options.D: Scaling makes Euclidean distance independent of units.

rationales.correct: k-NN commonly relies on distances; a feature measured in thousands can dominate one measured in fractions unless scaling or an alternative distance is used.
rationales.B: Standard k-NN does not learn a supervised rescaling automatically.
rationales.C: Scaling changes feature representation, not class labels.
rationales.D: Scaling can reduce unit dependence but does not make the distance intrinsically unit-independent.

stem: What does standardization using x' = (x - mean) / standard deviation primarily accomplish?

options.A: It centers each feature and expresses deviations in standard-deviation units, which can improve numerical conditioning for scale-sensitive algorithms.
options.B: It guarantees every feature is uniformly distributed.

rationales.correct: Standardization changes location and scale but does not enforce a distributional shape or remove dependence between features.
rationales.B: A z-score transformation does not make a feature uniform.
rationales.C: Outliers remain and can strongly influence mean and standard deviation.
rationales.D: Correlation structure is not generally eliminated by per-feature scaling.

stem: What is the primary objective of PCA?

options.A: Find orthogonal directions capturing decreasing amounts of variance and represent the data in a lower-dimensional coordinate system.
options.B: Maximize class-label separation using only the labels.
options.C: Guarantee every reduced feature is sparse.

rationales.correct: PCA is an unsupervised linear dimensionality-reduction method based on variance/covariance structure. The components are orthogonal directions ordered by explained variance.
rationales.C: PCA components are generally dense linear combinations.
rationales.D: P-values are not part of standard PCA.

stem: Why should PCA be fit only on the training portion inside a cross-validation pipeline?

options.A: The principal axes are learned from feature covariance, so fitting PCA on held-out data leaks information about the validation distribution.
options.B: PCA cannot operate on validation data.
options.C: PCA changes labels and therefore must be fit on y.

rationales.correct: PCA learns directions from the feature distribution. If those directions are computed using held-out folds, the representation of training examples has been informed by held-out information.
rationales.B: The fitted transformation can be applied to validation data after fitting on training data.
rationales.C: Standard PCA is unsupervised and does not need y.
rationales.D: Dimensionality reduction is commonly nested in a pipeline with CV.

stem: If PCA's first component explains 60% of the variance and the second explains 25%, what is the cumulative explained variance of the first two components?

rationales.correct: Cumulative explained variance is the sum of the component-wise explained variance ratios: 0.60 + 0.25 = 0.85.
rationales.A: This subtracts rather than adds the component ratios.

stem: A numeric feature contains extreme outliers. Which preprocessing choice is often more robust than mean/std standardization when the feature distribution is heavy-tailed?

options.A: A robust scaler based on statistics such as the median and interquartile range.
options.B: Replacing every value by its class label.
options.D: Multiplying the feature by a very large constant.

rationales.correct: Median and IQR are less sensitive to extreme values than mean and standard deviation, making robust scaling a common alternative for heavy-tailed data.
rationales.B: This discards the original feature and introduces target leakage if labels are used.
rationales.C: Ordering values does not normalize their scale.
rationales.D: A constant multiplier changes scale but does not fix outlier sensitivity.

stem: Which statement best describes one-hot encoding for a nominal categorical variable?

options.A: It represents categories as indicator columns without imposing an ordinal numeric relationship among the categories.
options.B: It assigns larger integers to imply stronger category membership.
options.C: It computes PCA scores for each category.
options.D: It necessarily reduces dimensionality to one feature.

rationales.correct: One-hot encoding creates binary indicators. Unlike ordinal encoding, the integer labels do not suggest that category 3 is 'more' than category 1.
rationales.B: That describes a potential problem with naive integer/ordinal encoding for nominal categories.
rationales.C: PCA is unrelated to the encoding definition.
rationales.D: One-hot encoding usually increases the feature count.

stem: A feature has 40% missing values, and missingness itself may indicate a meaningful operational state. Which design can preserve that signal without blindly imputing it away?

options.A: Impute a chosen value and add an explicit missing-indicator feature when the fact of missingness may be predictive.
options.B: Delete every row containing a missing value regardless of sample size.
options.C: Replace missing values with the target label.
options.D: Fill missing values using the full dataset after the test set is scored.

rationales.correct: An imputed value alone can hide the distinction between observed values and structural missingness. A missingness indicator can let the model learn that distinction. The imputation parameters themselves should be learned on training data within the pipeline.
rationales.B: Dropping rows can discard large amounts of data and create selection bias.
rationales.C: Using y to fill X leaks target information.
rationales.D: Test data must remain isolated from training transformations.
